title: The Aperture at the Pole: County Down, the Decorator's Desk, and the Interior World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: County Down, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested only by Bradshaw's own entry in Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124, which he supplied himself; later reference works repeat it. No town, parish, or townland within County Down has been located and no baptismal record found. The widely circulated claim that he was brought to America in infancy is rejected as mistaken by the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, and is contradicted by his Irish schooling, his 1877 prize, his 1878 appointment, and his children's Belfast births.
stops.campa: William Richard Bradshaw is born in County Down on the fourteenth of January, four years after the worst of the famine and in the province that suffered it least. The family is Anglo-Irish by his own later account. No town is named in any record that survives him; the county is as close as the documents come. Everything known about his first thirty-two years passes through one funnel, the entry he wrote about himself at fifty for Who's Who in America. The book printed what he sent it.
suggested_refs: The Who's Who in America entry of 1901-1902, the sole source for Bradshaw's Irish years
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, 'Bradshaw, William R.' (John Clute)
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: Belfast, the general education
stops.date_confidence: no year is attested; 1860 is an ordering placeholder inside the childhood. The schooling rests on four words in the self-supplied Who's Who entry, 'ed. Belfast, Ireland,' with no institution named and no register found. Coordinate is the standing Belfast pin.
stops.campa: Belfast in the eighteen-sixties is a linen town going over to shipbuilding, its population doubling inside a generation, its institutes turning out clerks and engineers and controversialists. Bradshaw is educated here. What the town gives him shows up later in the habits rather than the certificates: platform speaking, prize essays, debating rooms, the assumption that a young man with a good voice can make a living by using it. Which school, under whom, to what standard, the record does not say. It says Belfast.
suggested_refs: The Belfast institutes and literary associations of the 1860s, none of them named in Bradshaw's own account
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: South Kensington, the scientific course
stops.date_confidence: self-reported and undated; 1871 is an ordering placeholder between the Belfast schooling and the 1877 prize. The Who's Who entry says only 'took scientific course South Kensington, London' and names no college, syllabus, or qualification. No register entry has been found, and the attendance itself is unverified.
stops.campa: On the ground bought with the profits of the Great Exhibition the government has planted a quarter of science and art schools, museums, and lecture theatres. Bradshaw crosses to London and takes a course there; twenty years on he will be the American trade press's authority on the manufacture of paint. He names no college and claims no degree. Behind that one clause of his own there is only a young Irishman in a South Kensington lecture room, learning what a machine is, what a pigment is, what the earth is made of.
suggested_refs: The South Kensington government science and art schools, built on the Great Exhibition estate
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
Wikipedia, 'South Kensington'

stops.name: Belfast, the art of reading under Denis Leonard
stops.date_confidence: self-reported and undated; 1873 orders the segment. Denis Leonard, described in the Who's Who entry as 'Irish comedian and lawyer,' has not been independently identified in any source reached. The Irish press contributions Bradshaw claims have not been traced to a single byline.
stops.campa: He studies the art of reading under Denis Leonard. This is elocution as a discipline: breath, stress, the management of a hall without amplification, the timing that makes a paragraph land. Bradshaw works in Ireland as an essayist, debater, and dramatic reader, and writes for the Irish press on Irish character and travel. Not one of those pieces has been found under his name, and the teacher is gone as well, described in the Who's Who entry in four words and nowhere else: "Irish comedian and lawyer."
suggested_refs: The Victorian elocution manuals and dramatic-reading circuit of provincial Ireland
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124

stops.name: Ulster Hall, the gold medal for The Ulsterman
stops.date_confidence: the prize is attested only in Bradshaw's own Who's Who entry, which gives the year 1877 and the essay title 'The Ulsterman.' No copy of the essay and no award notice has been located in any catalogue reached. The venue is undocumented: the Ulster Hall coordinate is a reconstruction standing for the customary Belfast civic hall of such ceremonies, not a confirmed site.
stops.campa: The Church of Ireland Young Men's Association sets a prize essay and Bradshaw wins its gold medal, writing on the Ulsterman: the type, the character, the man of the province, described to a room of the province's own young men. It is his first recorded success and the only literary honour Ireland will give him. No copy of the essay survives in any catalogue reached, and no award notice has been found. The title, the year and the medal all come from his own Who's Who entry of 1901.
suggested_refs: The Ulster Hall, Bedford Street, Belfast, opened 1862; venue offered as reconstruction only
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
Wikipedia, 'Ulster Hall'

stops.name: Belfast, commissioner for taking affidavits
stops.date_confidence: self-reported in the Who's Who entry, dated 1878; the appointing instrument has not been located. The office is a legal-administrative commission and is not evidence that Bradshaw practised as barrister or solicitor, a distinction later summaries blur.
stops.campa: He is appointed a commissioner for taking affidavits for Belfast and County Antrim. The office is a small one: a man empowered to administer an oath and witness a sworn statement, so that the paper carries weight in a court he does not himself plead in. He is twenty-seven, and this is the only public office Ireland ever gives him. Forty-two years later, in Queens County, New York, he will stand on the other side of the same transaction, swearing before a notary to what a cancer researcher said from a Brooklyn stage, and signing himself with letters no record supports.
suggested_refs: The office of commissioner for taking affidavits in nineteenth-century Irish practice
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124

stops.name: Dublin, the marriage to Emma Douglas
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open. Bradshaw's own Who's Who entry reads 'm. Dublin, 1878, Emma Douglas'; later genealogical indexes give 1877. The civil marriage register entry has not been located by anyone consulted, and the bride's surname appears as both Douglas and Douglass. The date shown follows the self-report and is not adjudicated.
stops.campa: He marries Emma Douglas in Dublin. She will outlive him, is named in his obituary as his survivor almost fifty years later, and is otherwise missing from the record: no parents, no birth year, no letters, no photograph, not even a settled spelling of her name, which is Douglas in his account and Douglass in the indexes. Two sources give two different years for the wedding, his own and a later index, and neither has the register behind it. The marriage produces at least six children, of whom five are alive when he dies.
suggested_refs: The Irish civil marriage registers for Dublin, 1877 and 1878, unsearched for this entry
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
later genealogical indexes as relayed in the research dossier

stops.name: Strandtown, the birth of Mary Christobel
stops.date_confidence: a Belfast civil birth index entry naming William R. Bradshaw as father, relayed through the research dossier and not independently retrieved. The given name appears as both Christobel and Christabel. She later used the married surname Hansel and died in 1970.
stops.campa: A daughter is born at Strandtown, on the eastern edge of Belfast where the town runs out into villas and market gardens. The index gives her as Mary Christobel and gives her father as William R. Bradshaw. If the marriage was in 1878 she arrives within months of it; if it was 1877, within the year. She lives until 1970, ninety-two years, long enough to have seen her father's one novel serialised again in an American fantasy digest. Nothing she said about him, or about anything else, has come down.
suggested_refs: The Belfast civil birth index, Strandtown district, June 1878
sources: Belfast civil birth index entry as relayed in the research dossier
Wikipedia, 'Strandtown'

stops.name: Belfast, the birth of Reginald Douglas
stops.date_confidence: birth date from a genealogical and memorial record relayed through the dossier, not independently retrieved. Reginald died 7 January 1980 and was one of the two sons surviving his father in 1927. The family's Belfast address in 1881 is not recorded in anything reached.
stops.campa: A son, Reginald Douglas, is born in Belfast and takes his mother's family name for a middle one. He is the last of the Bradshaw children born in Ireland. His father is thirty, with a gold medal, a legal commission, a wife, two small children, and no book. Where in Belfast the household was living that October no reachable document says, and no street or house has been attached to the family in the year of this birth. Reginald lives until the seventh of January 1980, ninety-eight years old, outliving his father by fifty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Belfast birth registers of 1881
sources: genealogical and memorial record as relayed in the research dossier

stops.name: Castle Garden, the landing
stops.date_confidence: the year 1883 is Bradshaw's own, given in the Who's Who entry and repeated by later reference works. No passenger manifest has been found under his name and no month, port, or vessel is known. Castle Garden is a reconstruction: it was the working immigrant landing depot for New York until 1890 and is the likeliest point of arrival, not a documented one. Whether the family crossed together is unknown.
stops.campa: At thirty-two he emigrates. The old fort at the tip of Manhattan has been taking in immigrants for thirty years, thousands a day in season, run under its round roof and turned out onto the Battery. He arrives an adult, with a wife, children, a gold medal, a legal commission, and a trade in speaking, into a country where none of it counts for anything yet. Whatever later accounts say, no infant is carried over here. Some ship puts him ashore in 1883. No passenger list has been found with his name on it, and no month, port or vessel is known.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden, the New York immigrant landing depot in use 1855-1890
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: Chicago, the chair at Literary Life
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Who's Who entry reads 'editor of Literary Life, Chicago, 1886-7'; Wikipedia lists the magazine among his editorships but names no city and gives no dates, so both the Chicago placement and the years rest on the unread self-report. No office address is known and the coordinate is the standing central Chicago pin.
stops.campa: His first identified American work is an editor's chair at a magazine called Literary Life, and the only account of it is one clause he wrote about himself fifteen years afterward. Salary unknown, proprietor unknown, circulation unknown, office unknown, reason for leaving unknown. Chicago in the middle eighteen-eighties is rebuilding upward and printing at volume, and a literate Irishman with platform experience can find a desk in it. Two years later the family is in Brooklyn.
suggested_refs: Literary Life, the Chicago magazine of the 1880s, no run of which was located for this entry
sources: Who's Who in America, vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: Brooklyn, the son who does not survive
stops.date_confidence: the weakest item in the file. A son, William Clanmorna Bradshaw, is inferred to have died in early childhood from the gap between six recorded births and the five children reported as surviving in 1927. No death record, notice, or burial has been found; the date, the place, and the fact itself are reconstruction.
stops.campa: Six children are recorded born to William and Emma Bradshaw. Five are alive when he dies. The one who is not is named William Clanmorna, a name Irish in shape that matches no place and no family in any gazetteer reached. Everything else about him is a subtraction: no notice, no grave found, no year, no sentence anywhere in his father's own account of himself. He is in the record because six minus five is one. Whether he was born in Ireland or in America, and whether he reached his first birthday, nothing reached says.
suggested_refs: Brooklyn and Queens burial registers of the late 1880s, unsearched for this name
sources: inference from the gap between recorded births and the survivors named in the 1927 obituary

stops.name: Brooklyn, the birth of Wilmar Hereward
stops.date_confidence: birth record relayed through the dossier and not independently retrieved. A local-history page attributing Wilmar to a different William R. Bradshaw who died in 1888 is a documented source conflation and is not used here. Wilmar died 28 March 1975.
stops.campa: A son is born in Brooklyn and named Wilmar Hereward, which is the naming habit of a man already in the business of inventing proper nouns. Emma has now borne six children on two continents in eleven years. The family is east, inside the orbit of the New York trade press, and the father is a year away from the job that will occupy the rest of his working life and from the desk at which he writes his novel. Wilmar goes into the cigar and tobacco business and lives until 1975.
suggested_refs: The Brooklyn birth records of April 1889
sources: memorial and genealogical birth record as relayed in the research dossier

stops.name: New York, the editor's chair
stops.date_confidence: attested: issue front matter of The Decorator and Furnisher prints 'W. R. Bradshaw, Editor,' and the 1890-1896 span is independently confirmed. The exact office address has not been found; the coordinate is placed generically in the Manhattan publishing district of the period.
stops.campa: The Decorator and Furnisher is a monthly for the men who fit out other people's houses: upholsterers, cabinetmakers, wallpaper firms, architects working the American interior. Bradshaw takes the editor's chair and holds it six years. He does not only edit. He writes the paper, over his own initials, on paint chemistry and Moorish arches and Gobelin weave and the arrangement of a salon, an Ulster elocutionist made an authority on the decorative arts by the ordinary route of publishing monthly until nobody argues.
suggested_refs: The bound volumes of The Decorator and Furnisher, 1890-1896, with 'W. R. Bradshaw, Editor' on the front matter
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher, issue front matter and signed bylines as catalogued
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: New York, the manufacture of paints
stops.date_confidence: attested by signed byline, 'The Manufacture of Paints,' The Decorator and Furnisher, April 1890, as catalogued; the issue itself was not independently retrieved. 'New Effects in Decoration' had appeared under the same byline in March.
stops.campa: In April he publishes on the manufacture of paints: pigment, grinding, the oils, what the trade actually does before a colour ever reaches a wall. The month before, it had been new effects in decoration. This is the working rhythm of six years, a signed article or several every month on whatever the trade needs explained, and his readers are upholsterers and cabinetmakers who would know at once if he had it wrong. His only claimed training is a South Kensington course he never named to anybody.
suggested_refs: 'The Manufacture of Paints,' The Decorator and Furnisher, April 1890
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher, signed bylines as catalogued

stops.name: Saratoga Springs, the Pompeia
stops.date_confidence: the article, 'The Pompeia, Saratoga Springs,' The Decorator and Furnisher 16 no. 5, August 1890, is catalogued but was not independently retrieved, and it does not prove Bradshaw travelled to see the building. The Pompeia was Franklin W. Smith's Pompeian-revival hall on Broadway, begun 1888 and completed 1889; its exact site is not established and the coordinate is an approximate Broadway placement. It is not the Canfield Casino in Congress Park, with which it is often confused.
stops.campa: At the spa town a Boston hardware merchant named Franklin W. Smith has built a full-scale Pompeian house, two hundred feet by seventy-five, worked up out of Bulwer-Lytton's Last Days of Pompeii and opened the summer before. Bradshaw writes it up for his readers: the court, the colour, the archaeology turned into a building somebody can walk through in New York State. Whether he walked through it himself or worked from photographs and the builder's own literature, the article does not say.
suggested_refs: The Pompeia, Broadway, Saratoga Springs, built by Franklin W. Smith 1888-1889, partly burned 1926
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher 16, no. 5 (August 1890), as catalogued
Wikipedia, 'Franklin W. Smith'

stops.name: New York, the Gobelin tapestry
stops.date_confidence: the article on the Gobelin tapestry presented to the French Benevolent Society of New York is catalogued in The Decorator and Furnisher 17 no. 1, October 1890, and was not independently retrieved. The society's 1890 address has not been established, so the stop sits at the editorial-office coordinate rather than at a guessed street pin.
stops.campa: A Gobelin tapestry is presented to the French Benevolent Society of New York and Bradshaw writes it up for the October number: the weave, the cartoon, the descent of the manufacture from the royal workshops on the river Bievre. Where he stood to look at the thing cannot now be said, the society's address in 1890 having not been found in any source reached. He names the material and he names the provenance, and he leaves the admiration to the reader.
suggested_refs: The Gobelin tapestry presented to the Societe Francaise de Bienfaisance of New York, 1890
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher 17, no. 1 (October 1890), as catalogued

stops.name: St. Augustine, the Villa Zorayda
stops.date_confidence: the article, 'The Villa Zorayda at St. Augustine, Florida,' The Decorator and Furnisher, March 1891, is catalogued but was not independently retrieved. Whether Bradshaw travelled to Florida or worked from photographs and press material is not established. Coordinate is the building itself, 83 King Street.
stops.campa: Franklin W. Smith again, this time in Florida: a house at 83 King Street poured in concrete and coquina from 1883, its courts and arches copied from the Alhambra, finished before Flagler's hotels made the town a resort. Bradshaw describes it for the trade. Moorish arcades, tiled surfaces, an interior organised around a court instead of a hall. He is a year from publishing a novel whose imagined civilisation is furnished almost entirely out of this vocabulary.
suggested_refs: The Villa Zorayda, 83 King Street, St. Augustine, Florida, built by Franklin W. Smith from 1883
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher 17 (March 1891), as catalogued
Wikipedia, 'Villa Zorayda'

stops.name: New York, the interview with Napoleon Sarony
stops.date_confidence: attested by signed byline, 'The Nude in Art: An Interview with Napoleon Sarony,' The Decorator and Furnisher, June 1895, as catalogued; the issue was not independently retrieved.
stops.campa: He interviews Napoleon Sarony, the photographer who turned the celebrity portrait into an American industry and who carried his own case to the Supreme Court to establish that a photograph can be copyrighted at all. The subject is the nude in art, a question the decorating trade cares about because its clients hang pictures on the walls it sells them. Bradshaw asks, and prints the answers, and does not put his own opinion in the way. He leaves the magazine the following year.
suggested_refs: 'The Nude in Art: An Interview with Napoleon Sarony,' The Decorator and Furnisher, June 1895
sources: The Decorator and Furnisher, signed bylines as catalogued

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the copyright entered
stops.date_confidence: attested from the book's own front matter, independently re-fetched in the Project Gutenberg digitisation of the first edition: copyright notice 1891 by William R. Bradshaw, title page dated 1892, imprint 'J. F. Douthitt, 286 Fifth Avenue, New York.' Coordinate is that street address, between 30th and 31st Streets. The quotation is the novel's opening sentence, verbatim.
stops.campa: In the middle of the editorship he writes a novel and enters it for copyright. The publisher is J. F. Douthitt of 286 Fifth Avenue, a house better known for art books than for fiction. The title runs the length of a paragraph: The Goddess of Atvatabar, Being the History of the Discovery of the Interior World and Conquest of Atvatabar. It is the only book securely his, and it is the reason anybody opens his name now. The copyright is stamped 1891 and the title page reads 1892.
stops.quote: What was the cause that startled the polar midnight with such unwonted commotion?
stops.quote_source: The Goddess of Atvatabar (1892), chapter I, Project Gutenberg eBook 32825
suggested_refs: The J. F. Douthitt imprint at 286 Fifth Avenue, New York
sources: Project Gutenberg eBook 32825, front matter and text of the first edition

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the gulf at the pole
stops.date_confidence: the descent of the premise is attested: the San Francisco Morning Call review of 5 June 1892 invokes 'Symmes' Hole' by name, and the novel's own text carries the polar aperture. The review is relayed through the dossier and was not independently refetched. The quotation is verbatim from the Project Gutenberg text of the first edition. No statement by Bradshaw naming Symmes as his source has been located.
stops.campa: The yacht Polar King sails north and finds, instead of ice, an opening. Bradshaw takes the premise whole from John Cleves Symmes Jr., the Ohio infantry captain who spent the eighteen-twenties lecturing that the earth is hollow and open at both poles and petitioning Congress to fund an expedition into it. Symmes died in 1829, twenty-two years before Bradshaw was born, and no statement by Bradshaw naming him has been located. The San Francisco Morning Call spots the descent anyway and calls it Symmes's Hole.
stops.quote: The North Pole is an immense gulf 500 miles in diameter and of unknown depth.
stops.quote_source: The Goddess of Atvatabar (1892), Project Gutenberg eBook 32825
suggested_refs: Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres (1826) and the polar-aperture doctrine
The San Francisco Morning Call review of 5 June 1892, which names Symmes's Hole
sources: Project Gutenberg eBook 32825
San Francisco Morning Call, 5 June 1892, as catalogued

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the introduction by Julian Hawthorne
stops.date_confidence: attested from the book's front matter, independently confirmed in the Project Gutenberg text: the introduction is by Julian Hawthorne, and it sets the book against Jules Verne and Bulwer-Lytton. The February date orders the segment and marks nothing in the record. Julian Hawthorne has no separate biography in this corpus.
stops.campa: The book opens not in Bradshaw's voice but in Julian Hawthorne's. The son of Nathaniel Hawthorne, by then a working novelist and reviewer with a name to lend, writes an introduction placing the thing in a line: against Jules Verne, whose voyages go under the earth by machinery, and against Bulwer-Lytton, whose Coming Race found a superior people already living down there. Inside Bradshaw's front matter, Hawthorne uses the space to argue idealist romance against the naturalism then taking the field in American fiction.
stops.quote: Spirit is the substance; fact the shadow only, and its whole claim to existence lies in its relation to spirit.
stops.quote_source: Julian Hawthorne, Introduction to The Goddess of Atvatabar (1892)
suggested_refs: Julian Hawthorne's introduction to The Goddess of Atvatabar, 1892
sources: Project Gutenberg eBook 32825, introduction

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the plates
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open. The book's own list of illustrations runs to 32 entries, a frontispiece map and 31 plates, correcting the 'forty-five plates' repeated by booksellers. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction states that the first issue of the 1892 printing lacked the pictorial elements and that they appear in the second issue; the bookseller descriptions of an illustrated first edition are not reconciled with that here. The March date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Eight artists are credited on the title page, C. Durand Chapman first among them, then R. W. Rattray, Carl Gutherz, Harold Haven Brown, Paul de Longpre, Leonard M. Davis, Walter M. Dunk, and Allan B. Doggett. They draw the throne room, the aerial ships, the goddess. Booksellers have described the first edition for a century as profusely illustrated with forty-five plates. The book's own list of illustrations has thirty-two, and the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction holds that the earliest issue had no pictures in it at all.
suggested_refs: The Houghton Library copy, SF-251, whose cover, title page and sixteen plates are digitised on Wikimedia Commons
sources: Project Gutenberg eBook 32825, list of illustrations
The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, 'Bradshaw, William R.'
Wikimedia Commons, 'Category:William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the invented tongue
stops.date_confidence: quotation verbatim from the Project Gutenberg text of the first edition, chapter X. The April date orders the segment and marks nothing in the record. 'Professor Starbottle, Astronomer' is independently confirmed in the ship's company list and chapter V of the same text.
stops.campa: Inside the aperture is a world with its own sun, its own sky, its own physics and its own language, and Bradshaw supplies all of it as he goes. The first Atvatabarese the expedition meets comes down through the air shouting. He supplies the theology too, a religion of twin souls presided over by the goddess Lyone, and the machinery: aerial ships, pneumatic transit, a motive power he calls magnicity. Gravity he settles in a clause, on the principle that weight is caused by an object having the world on one side of it.
stops.quote_source: The Goddess of Atvatabar (1892), chapter X, Project Gutenberg eBook 32825

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the hymn to Lyone
stops.date_confidence: quotation verbatim from the Project Gutenberg text of the first edition, first stanza of the in-novel hymn 'To Lyone.' The May date orders the segment and marks nothing in the record.
stops.campa: At the centre of the interior world is a living goddess and a cult of the twin soul, love held at a pitch just short of consummation and made the engine of an entire civilisation. The Ulster prize essayist and paint-manufacture correspondent writes hymns for her, in metre, at length, and prints them in the book under the title To Lyone. The plot ends with the interior world conquered and the goddess married off to the explorer. The first stanza had called her a jewel that lighteneth gloom, the soul of a lover invested with purest of clay, a chrysalis eager to hover and fly from her prison away.
stops.quote: Oh goddess, oh deity glorious, With golden wan face, and the bloom Of spirit and figure victorious! Oh jewel that lighteneth gloom, Men call thee the soul of a lover, Invested with purest of clay, A chrysalis, eager to hover And fly from thy prison away!
stops.quote_source: The Goddess of Atvatabar (1892), hymn 'To Lyone,' stanza I, Project Gutenberg eBook 32825
suggested_refs: The hymn 'To Lyone' and the twin-soul theology of Atvatabar
sources: Project Gutenberg eBook 32825

stops.name: 286 Fifth Avenue, the notices
stops.date_confidence: three contemporary reviews are catalogued and relayed through the dossier without independent refetching: St. Paul Daily Globe, 5 May 1892; the Sun, New York, 4 June 1892; San Francisco Morning Call, 5 June 1892. The stop sits at the publisher's address because the reviewing was done elsewhere and by other hands; it records the book's reception, not a place Bradshaw went. The promised sequel is reported by later summaries and no trace of one has been found.
stops.campa: St. Paul laughs and files it with Verne and Munchausen. The Sun in New York denies that it servilely imitates Haggard's She while suggesting that She stands behind it, and makes sport of the prose. San Francisco names Symmes's Hole outright and praises the invented machinery and the plates. Nobody calls it a bad book. Nobody calls it a good one. It sells no second novel, no publisher asks for one, and the sequel Bradshaw is said to have promised is nowhere in the record at all.
suggested_refs: St. Paul Daily Globe, 5 May 1892; the Sun, New York, 4 June 1892; San Francisco Morning Call, 5 June 1892
sources: digitised newspaper reviews as catalogued in the research dossier

stops.name: Flushing, the move out
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1927 obituary and later summaries agree that Bradshaw left The Decorator and Furnisher in 1896 and lived in Flushing from that year until his death. The obituary clipping was not independently refetched.
stops.campa: He gives up the editorship and moves out to Flushing, then a village in Queens County with its own main street, a Quaker meeting house older than the republic, and a train into the city. He is forty-five, and no reason for his leaving the magazine is recorded on either side. He does not move again for thirty-one years. Everything after this happens from a Flushing address: the freelance decorating articles, the reference-book entry, the ward work, the vivisection fight, the affidavit, the funeral.
suggested_refs: Flushing, Queens, as a village on the eve of consolidation into New York City
sources: 1927 obituary as relayed in the research dossier
Wikipedia, 'William R. Bradshaw'

stops.name: New York, the salon and the carpets
stops.date_confidence: signed articles catalogued in The Art Amateur: 'The House. The Salon.' in October and November 1898 and January 1899, and 'Carpets and Rugs' in February 1899. The issues were not independently retrieved and the magazine's editorial address is placed generically in the Manhattan publishing district.
stops.campa: Out of the chair, he goes on writing the same beat for a competitor. The Art Amateur takes a series from him on the salon, then on carpets and rugs: what a room is for, where the chairs go, what is under them. He is nearly fifty, with a novel behind him that no publisher followed up and an invented civilisation nobody bought twice, and the money is still in upholstery. The last of the series runs in February 1899. After it, his byline goes quiet for eleven years.
suggested_refs: 'The House. The Salon.' and 'Carpets and Rugs,' The Art Amateur, 1898-1899
sources: The Art Amateur, signed articles as catalogued

stops.name: 57 Locust Street, the entry in Who's Who
stops.date_confidence: the entry appears in Who's Who in America vol. 2 (1901-1902), p. 124, verified against the Internet Archive OCR text of that volume. It is self-supplied and is the sole source for most of Bradshaw's Irish life. The quotation restores the closing sentences usually dropped, including the Flushing residence, which is what ties this man to the 'Dr. William R. Bradshaw of Flushing, N.Y.' of the 1920 affidavit; the ellipsis marks the omitted middle.
stops.campa: He fills in the form. Everything known of his first thirty-two years enters the record here, in a paragraph of abbreviations he wrote about himself: the county, the date, the schools, the medal, the commission, the wife, the crossing, the two editorships, the one novel. There is no independent document behind most of it, and every later account of his life copies this page. The paragraph ends with an address, 57 Locust St., Flushing, N. Y., which is the line later quotations usually drop.

stops.name: Flushing, the district captain
stops.date_confidence: the 1927 obituary and later summaries describe Bradshaw as a Republican district captain in Flushing; no year, term, candidacy, elected office, or campaign controversy has been located. The 1905 date is an ordering placeholder.
stops.campa: A district captain is the smallest working unit of American political machinery, and the obituary gives Bradshaw's years of it a single clause. It suits a man trained since his twenties to hold a room by voice alone. No candidacy of his own is on record, no office sought, no quarrel reported, no term dated, no ward numbered. What is left is the work itself, which does not vary: canvassing, turning out the vote, knowing who lives behind which door on which street of Flushing and what will move them.

stops.name: Porcupine Lake, hunting for gold

Bradshaw publishes on it in Field and Stream, over his own name, at fifty-nine, eleven years after his last traced byline. Nothing else in the record puts him in Canada, or in a canoe, or within five hundred miles of a claim. His obituary will call him a former editor of the magazine, and no issue found names him as one.

stops.name: Albany, the fourteen-year bill
stops.date_confidence: the Frederic Schiller Lee papers at Columbia University are described as documenting a 1909-1923 dispute in which Bradshaw is a spokesman for the anti-vivisection party; the finding aid returned an access-denied page and could not be checked directly. The Albany placement is a reconstruction standing for the New York legislature: no single dated appearance by Bradshaw at the Capitol has been identified.
stops.campa: For fourteen years bills to restrict animal experiment are put before the New York legislature and beaten back by the medical faculties, whose organiser is the Columbia physiologist Frederic Schiller Lee. Bradshaw is one of the voices on the other side, named in Lee's own papers as a spokesman for the anti-vivisection party. He is fifty-eight when the dispute opens in 1909 and seventy-two when it ends in 1923. The Columbia finding aid that describes it returned an access-denied page and could not be read.

stops.name: Buffalo, the uselessness of vivisection
stops.date_confidence: a Buffalo News item of 11 April 1911 headed 'The Uselessness of Vivisection' is catalogued and was not independently retrieved. Whether Bradshaw spoke in Buffalo in person or the paper printed supplied text is not established.
stops.campa: A Buffalo paper carries The Uselessness of Vivisection under his name, four hundred miles from Flushing; whether he stood in the city or the paper printed text he supplied is not established. He is sixty. The argument he will make for the rest of his life is already in the title: not that the experiments are cruel and necessary, but that they are cruel and produce nothing. That is a claim about results rather than about mercy, and a claim about results can be checked.

stops.name: Flushing, the book that may not exist

Either the book is lost more completely than a 1914 book should be, or it was never printed at all.

stops.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music, the lecture on cancer
stops.date_confidence: attested only by Bradshaw's own sworn affidavit of 5 October 1920, which places him in the audience and reports Woglom's words. Woglom denied saying them in that form and the New York Anti-Vivisection Society afterwards withdrew the disputed paragraph. No transcript or press report of the lecture has been located. The quotation is Bradshaw's sworn version, not verified speech.
stops.campa: On a Saturday evening he goes to the Academy of Music in Brooklyn to hear Dr. William H. Woglom of the Crocker Research Laboratory speak on the latest developments in cancer research. Bradshaw is sixty-five and takes no notes that anyone has found. What he hears, or believes he hears, he sets down in the first person four and a half years later, under oath. No transcript of the lecture exists and no press report of it has been located. What was said in that hall cannot now be recovered.
stops.quote: Up to the present time, over a million and a half of animals have been sacrificed in the effort to discover the cause or provide a remedy for cancer, but neither the cause nor the cure has yet been discovered, and if any man says he has discovered a cure for cancer through animal experimentation, that man is a liar.

stops.name: Flushing, the paragraph withdrawn

stops.name: 37 Locust Street, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1927 obituaries give the date, the address, a brief illness, and the survivors, and the same language is quoted in later summaries; the clipping itself was not independently refetched. The obituary states his age as 75, which contradicts the January 1851 birth date by a year. The discrepancy is left open.
stops.campa: He dies at home on Locust Street on the nineteenth of July after what the papers call a brief illness. He is seventy-six by his own stated birth date and seventy-five by the obituary's arithmetic, and nobody at the time thinks the discrepancy worth checking. Emma survives him, with two sons and three daughters. The notices identify him as a former magazine editor, a Republican district captain, and a lecturer against vivisection. He had lived in the same few streets of Queens for thirty-one years.
